sites.name: Ashcroft Ghost Town
overview: Ashcroft is a preserved historic silver-mining town in the upper Castle Creek Valley, about eleven miles from Aspen.
Founded during the 1880 silver rush, the settlement grew quickly as a mining and transportation hub before shallow ore deposits and the rise of Aspen led to a rapid decline.

timeline.text: Prospectors Charles B. Culver and W. F. Coxhead found silver in the upper Castle Creek Valley. The camp first called Castle Forks City developed into Ashcroft.
Mining declined as shallow ore veins failed to sustain production. Residents increasingly moved to Aspen, and by 1912 fewer than 50 people remained.
The Highland Bavarian Lodge ski project incorporated Ashcroft, and during World War II the U.S. Army's 10th Mountain Division trained nearby.

Aspen Historical Society began stewarding the townsite under U.S. Forest Service permit. Restored and relocated historic structures, trails, interpretation, and surviving foundations preserve the site for visitors.

moreHistory: Aspen Historical Society identifies Ashcroft as an 1880s mining town and transportation junction at the headwaters of Castle Creek. Its surviving landscape includes restored and relocated log buildings, the original post office building in its original location, visible former building foundations, and other remnants of the settlement.
The town's boom was brief. Ashcroft's mines closed after ore veins proved to be shallow surface deposits, and many residents moved to Aspen, sometimes taking cabins with them.

For Remnant identification, the townsite destination point linked by Aspen Historical Society at approximately 39.0544504, -106.8000586 is used as the defensible Scan anchor for the historic townsite. This is a townsite-level anchor, not a claim for any single surviving building.

sites.name: Alpine Mine
overview: Alpine Mine is a documented historic gold mine in Pitkin County's Columbia (Ashcroft) mining district. USGS-derived topographic mapping preserves the named mine at approximately 39.049990, -106.797816, providing a defensible identification point without implying present-day access or surviving open workings.
moreHistory: Available retained sources consistently place this Alpine Mine in the Ashcroft-area Columbia mining district and distinguish it from same-name mines elsewhere in Colorado and Nevada. The current evidence supports the mine's identity, district, commodity, and mapped location, but does not establish a reliable operator chronology, production total, or surviving condition, so those details are left unstated.

sites.name: Aspen Mine
sites.componentDetail: Silver-Lead-Zinc Mine / Shaft and Connected Underground Workings
overview: The Aspen Mine was a major early silver property on Aspen Mountain. Discovered in 1884, it became central to the legal battle over whether a mineral vein's owner could follow the ore beneath neighboring claims.

The identification point follows the USGS-mapped Aspen Mine property in Vallejo Gulch. The historic mine included a shaft and an extensive connected system of drifts, levels, winzes, and tunnels; it does not identify a safe or accessible opening.

timeline.text: Elmer T. Butler and partners are credited with discovering the Aspen Mine.
A lease operated by Aspen mayor J. D. Hooper struck high-grade silver ore at about 120 feet, accelerating the district's boom.
The Aspen Mine became the focus of nationally watched apex-versus-sideline litigation over underground ore rights.
The competing interests reached a settlement that placed disputed holdings into the Compromise Mining Company and allowed development to resume.
USGS Map I-785-D documented the mine among Aspen-quadrangle silver, lead, and zinc producers and preserved its mapped property location.

moreHistory: USGS-derived records describe twelve mine levels developed at 50- and 100-foot intervals between roughly 400 and 1,200 feet deep, with extensive drifting along the Contact, Aspen, and subordinate faults.
The Lower Durant Tunnel, driven about 2,700 feet for drainage and ore transport, connected with the Durant-Aspen workings west of the Aspen shaft.
Mineral records list silver, zinc, and lead as the primary commodities and identify sphalerite and argentite among the ore minerals.

Later accounts describe portions of the old Aspen workings as connected to the broader Compromise/Durant underground network. Historic mine openings and underground spaces are hazardous, and this entry does not imply public access.

sites.name: Argentum-Juniata Mine
sites.location: Base of east Aspen Mountain near Aspen
sites.componentDetail: Silver-Lead-Zinc Mine Complex / Incline and Tunnel Workings
overview: The Argentum-Juniata was a major silver-era property at the base of east Aspen Mountain. Historic and mineral-resource records connect the property with the Juniata name, the Argenta Tunnel, the A-J Tunnel, and a group of claims and underground workings.

The identification point marks the documented Argentum-Juniata property and incline area. Historic maps and later records place related portals and workings close together, so it should not be read as a claim that one specific opening survives at that exact point.

timeline.text: A surviving Aspen Historical Society photograph documents the mine's compressor, boiler plant, and ore house.
The Argentum-Juniata operated during Aspen's major silver-mining period and was mapped as part of the district's connected underground mine network.
USGS Monograph 31 documented the geology and underground workings of the Aspen mining district, including the Argentum-Juniata property.
Federal mineral statistics reported siliceous silver ore with small lead values from the Argentum-Juniata.

moreHistory: Mineral-resource records list Argentum-Juniata Mine as the primary property name and treat Juniata, Argenta Tunnel, A-J Tunnel, and several named claims as associated names or workings.

The separately indexed Argentum-Juanita Incline lies only a short distance from the broader property coordinate and is treated here as a component of the same historic mine complex, not as an unrelated second destination.
The mine produced silver-bearing ore with lead and zinc associations. Period federal reporting specifically described its 1907 output as siliceous silver ore carrying small lead values.

Historic underground workings in Aspen are extensive and may intersect beneath developed areas. This entry identifies the historic property and does not imply access, ownership, or a safe surviving portal.
